extracted.intended_audience: literate general public and aspiring essayists/men of letters (readers of The Spectator interested in rhetoric, manners, and moral advice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative remarks for composing moral/rhetorical essays, letters, and tasteful depictions of passion and behaviour in the style of The Spectator; includes prescriptions about wit, pity, modesty, and self-examination. Useful for writers of short moral or social pieces and for commentators on manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning (the Punn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning...belongs to a Set of Mortals who value themselves upon an uncommon Mastery in the more humane and polite Part of Letters. This Mongrel miscreated (to speak in Miltonic) kind of Wit, vulgarly termed, the Punn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punning is presented as a low or mongrel wit that 'fills the Imagination with an Assemblage of such Ideas and Pictures as are hardly any thing but Shade' and may 'almost benight the Faculties.' Its social origins (at table, in certain company and atmospheres) are noted. Yet the author also allows that 'this humbler Exercise may be as instrumental in diverting us from any innovating Schemes and Hypothesis in Wit' — i.e., small puns can be a harmless diversion but should be avoided as a sign of shallow imagination or excessive enthusiastically displayed wit. Avoid excessive or ill-placed puns; be aware of social context; treat punning as lower wit even if occasionally defensible as diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity/Compassion in Rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion does not only refine and civilize Humane Nature... As Love is the most delightful Passion, Pity is nothing else but Love softned by a degree of Sorrow: In short, it is a kind of pleasing Anguish, as well as generous Sympathy, that knits Mankind together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce pity in readers, writers should cultivate genuine feeling rather than merely invent it. Those who 'lay down Rules for Rhetorick or Poetry, advise the Writer to work himself up, if possible, to the Pitch of Sorrow which he endeavours to produce in others.' Grief has a natural eloquence that outdoes artifice; authentic expressions of suffering (especially first‑person or factual accounts) move readers more than laboured fictional strokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and matter-of-fact over laboured fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are none therefore who stir up Pity so much as those who indite their own Sufferings. Grief has a natural Eloquence belonging to it... the short Speeches, or Sentences which we often meet with in Histories, make a deeper Impression on the Mind of the Reader, than the most laboured Strokes in a well-written Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer brief, factual, truthful accounts (letters, short speeches in histories) to elaborate fictional dramatization when aiming to affect the reader. Example: Queen Anne Boleyn's real last letter is held up as more affecting than any dramatic invention. Use concise, authentic detail to set the person before the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity (work yourself up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have laid down Rules for Rhetorick or Poetry, advise the Writer to work himself up, if possible, to the Pitch of Sorrow which he endeavours to produce in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer's internalization of the emotion they aim to convey produces more moving writing than simulated or merely technical efforts. Cultivate the feeling you wish the reader to feel rather than rely solely on rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty in depiction of desire ('the prevailing gentle Art')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedley has that prevailing gentle Art... Which, can with a resistless Charm impart The loosest Wishes to the chastest Heart... To soft Flutes The Silver Oars kept Time; and while they play'd, The Hearing gave new Pleasure to the Sight, And both to Thought...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To excite admiration or desire tastefully, employ gentleness, restraint, and artful conformity to modest manners rather than rustic bluntness or coarse expression. Dress the scene delicately, imply rather than display, and combine visual and aural suggestion (music, subtle movement) to warm the imagination without lapsing into explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid licentious language
rubrics_metrics.description: Licentious Language has something brutal in it, which disgraces Humanity, and leaves us in the Condition of the Savages in the Field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarse or explicit language degrades both subject and audience; to maintain civility and refined impact, avoid licentious phrasing. Preserve humanity and dignity in depiction; restraint is both morally and aesthetically preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical subtlety in courtship depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Much Care and Concern for the Lady's Welfare, to seem afraid lest she should be annoyed by the very Air which surrounds her, and this uttered rather with kind Looks, and expressed by an Interjection, an Ah, or an Oh, at some little Hazard in moving or making a Step, than in my direct Profession of Love, are the Methods of skilful Admirers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing seduction or courtship, prefer gestures, looks, small interjections, and simulated fear for the lady's welfare over direct professions. Subtlety and apparent concern are more effective (and more creditable) than bold advances; these devices can be used ethically or abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray cross-sex friendship with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Women may disguise it if they think fit... If a Man's Heart has not the Abhorrence of any treacherous Design, he may easily improve Approbation into Kindness, and Kindness into Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising or portraying friendships between men and women, recognise the real risk that esteem and kindness can slide into passion. Writers and moralists should warn readers (particularly women) to be cautious of close cross‑sex intimacy presented as purely platonic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for self-knowledge and detecting hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: I would therefore propose the following Methods... let them consider well what are the Characters which they bear among their Enemies... how far we may deserve the Praises and Approbations which the World bestow upon us... not lay too great a Stress on any supposed Virtues we possess that are of a doubtful Nature... be very apprehensive of those Actions which proceed from natural Constitution, favourite Passions, particular Education, or whatever promotes our worldly Interest or Advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To discover secret faults and avoid self-deceit: (1) weigh criticisms from enemies as revealing hidden flaws; (2) examine whether public praise arises from worthy motives; (3) be cautious about virtues that many doubt or that align with partisan zeal; (4) suspect actions driven by temperament, passion, upbringing, or self‑interest. Use these methods as checks in moral self-examination and when portraying believable characters who are self‑deceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exempla (historical letters) for pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not remember to have seen any Ancient or Modern Story more affecting than a Letter of Ann of Bologne... which is still extant... written by her own Hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing authentic historical documents or quoted letters can supply immediate pathos and credibility. Such exempla place the subject before the reader and often move more effectively than contrived fiction; use them when available and relevant.
